candidates.label: Near Tel Shalem, south of Beth-shean (Scythopolis)
candidates.support: The early Christian writer Eusebius, in his Onomasticon, places Aenon eight Roman miles south of Scythopolis (modern Beit She'an), near a place he calls Salumias. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia judges this "the most probable" identification: it locates Salim itself at Tell Ridhghah, beside a shrine known locally as Sheikh Selim, with springs "not far off, by the ruins of Umm el-'Amdan" that, in its reading, "exactly suit the position indicated by" Eusebius. No independently confirmed coordinate exists for that exact ruin, so this candidate uses the nearby, well-documented site of Tel Shalem, a few kilometers away in the same district south of Beit She'an, as the nearest point an accepted source records, corroborated by Pleiades' point for Salem/Salumias, 65 meters away.

candidates.label: Wadi al-Kharrar, east of the Jordan (the Madaba Map's "Ainon")
candidates.support: The sixth-century Madaba mosaic map (so dated by its own Wikidata record) labels a site at the start of Wadi al-Kharrar, east of the Jordan, with a name meaning "the place of Willows," which, according to Michele Piccirillo's study of the map, the map itself equates with Ainon; the seventh-century writer John Moschus likewise locates the same place, near a monastic settlement, close to the Jordan, in Piccirillo's account of his record. OpenBible.info's ancient-place catalog also records this identification, under its own listing for "Aenon," with less confidence than the catalog's higher-ranked candidate, Khirbet Einun, recorded below as an unmapped candidate. This point lies close to, but is not identical with, the separate Al-Maghtas candidate this project records for Bethany beyond the Jordan (John 1:28).

unmappedCandidates.label: 'Ainun (Khirbet Einun), east of Nablus
unmappedCandidates.support: Some explorers, including Edward Robinson and Claude Conder, proposed 'Ainun in Wady Far'ah, with the village of Salim east of Nablus six miles away, as the site of Aenon and Salim; OpenBible.info's ancient-place catalog records this identification among its candidates. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia argues against it: the site "is in the very heart of Samaria, and therefore impossible," and adds that Aenon's position, defined by its six-mile distance from Salim with a high ridge between them, "would hardly be defined by the village of Salim, with the important city of Shechem quite as near, and more easily accessible."
unmappedCandidates.reason: No accepted source gives a coordinate for 'Ainun/Khirbet Einun itself; the only recorded point traces to GeoNames, which this project does not use as a coordinate source. The village of Salim, six miles away by the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia's own figure, has an accepted coordinate, but it is not itself the proposed site of Aenon.

summary.text: Aenon near Salim is the place where, according to John's Gospel, John the Baptist was baptizing "because there was much water there," at a time when Jesus and his disciples were in the land of Judea, baptizing. The World English Bible spells the name "Enon." Its location is disputed: the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia favors a district south of Beth-shean (Scythopolis), following the writer Eusebius, while a separate tradition, recorded on the Madaba mosaic map, places an "Ainon" east of the Jordan; other proposals, including a site called 'Ainun east of Nablus, in Samaria, have no coordinate from an accepted source.

history.text: John's Gospel immediately adds that "John was not yet thrown into prison," and records a dispute arising between John's disciples and some Jews about purification, after which John's disciples tell him that Jesus, whom John had earlier pointed to, "baptizes, and everyone is coming to him"; John answers, "He must increase, but I must decrease."

scripture.textWEB: John also was baptizing in Enon near Salim, because there was much water there. They came and were baptized;

politicalHistory.entity: Roman province of Syria (Scythopolis, a Decapolis city, answerable to the governor of Syria)
politicalHistory.note: The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia's article on Salim states that this district "did not belong to Samaria, but was included in the lands of Scythopolis, which was an important member of the league of ten cities"; its article on the Decapolis describes Scythopolis, the only one of the ten cities west of the Jordan, as independent of the local tetrarchy and answerable directly to the governor of Syria, dating the league's constitution to about the time of the Roman general Pompey's campaign in the region, 65 BC. This map starts the entry in 63 BC to match other Decapolis-area entries.

politicalHistory.entity: Kingdom of Herod the Great (ruler: Herod the Great)
Tetrarchy of Galilee and Perea (ruler: Herod Antipas)
Kingdom of Herod Agrippa I (ruler: Herod Agrippa I)

politicalHistory.note: The emperor Nero later added the Galilean towns of Tiberias and Taricheae (identified with Magdala), and Julias in Perea with fourteen villages, to Agrippa II's kingdom; the Jewish historian Josephus dates this to AD 54, but the Jewish Encyclopedia (1906) reads Agrippa II's coinage as pointing to AD 61 instead. These are towns, not land of their own, so this area's extent does not change.

politicalHistory.entity: Roman province of Judea (ruler: Legates, with a legion now based at Jerusalem)
politicalHistory.note: An administrative upgrade (a legate instead of a procurator), not a border or name change.
